nature-eco-190.title: Photosynthesis: how sunlight becomes food and oxygen
nature-eco-190.text: The living world captures sunlight at a rate of about 130 terawatts, roughly eight times the power used by human civilization. The machinery doing this is photosynthesis: the process by which plants, algae and cyanobacteria turn light energy, usually from the sun, into chemical energy. These are the autotrophs met in {{ref:nature-eco-324}}, the organisms that make their own food. In its usual form, called oxygenic photosynthesis, the process splits water and releases oxygen. The captured energy is stored in carbon compounds such as sugars, starch and cellulose. Cells later break these compounds down through {{ref:nature-eco-212}} to get the energy back. The scale is immense. Each year photosynthetic organisms turn around 100–115 billion tons of carbon into biomass, the stuff of living bodies. The consequences reach far beyond any single leaf. Oxygen released by cyanobacteria long ago filled Earth's air, which made complex life possible. Photosynthesis still produces and maintains that oxygen today, and it supplies most of the energy that complex life runs on. The name is surprisingly recent: Charles Reid Barnes proposed it in 1893.

nature-eco-173.title: Biogeochemical cycles: the planet's recycling loops
nature-eco-173.text: Nothing in an ecosystem is ever truly used up. A biogeochemical cycle is the movement and transformation of chemical elements and compounds between living things, the air and the Earth's crust. Energy and matter behave differently here. Energy flows one way through an ecosystem: it arrives as sunlight and leaves as heat. The matter that makes up living things is instead conserved and recycled. Six elements common in living matter take many chemical forms as they move: carbon, nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur. The major cycles include those of carbon, nitrogen and water. In each one, living things change and move a substance, which also passes through stores such as the air, the soil and the oceans. Microorganisms drive much of this cycling. Rocks take part too. Weathering, erosion, drainage and plate subduction, the slow sinking of one slab of Earth's crust beneath another, all help recycle materials. That mix of life, geology and chemistry is why the cycles are called biogeochemical. Today global warming and other human impacts are changing the speed, intensity and balance of many of them.

nature-eco-164.title: The carbon cycle: life's main ingredient on the move
nature-eco-164.text: The soil underfoot holds about 1,500 gigatons of carbon, a gigaton being a billion tons. All the plants and other organisms above ground hold about 500 gigatons. Carbon is the main ingredient of living matter and a major part of many rocks, such as limestone. The carbon cycle is the exchange of carbon among living things, soils, rocks, water and the air of Earth. It covers both the quick recycling of carbon through living things and its long-term storage in, and release from, the natural stores described in {{ref:nature-eco-169}}. In the air, carbon exists mainly as carbon dioxide and methane. Both gases trap heat and drive part of the warming explained in {{ref:nature-eco-161}}. Carbon dioxide leaves the air mainly through photosynthesis, entering life on land and in the ocean. In 2024 the global average level of carbon dioxide in the air reached a record 422.7 parts per million. The steps of this cycle are key to making Earth able to support life. Antoine Lavoisier and Joseph Priestley first described it, and Humphry Davy popularised it.

nature-eco-196.title: The water cycle: one supply, endlessly moving
nature-eco-196.text: Earth's total mass of water stays fairly constant. What changes with the climate is how that water is split between ice, fresh water, salt water and air. The water cycle, or hydrologic cycle, is the continuous movement of water on, above and below the Earth's surface, as it changes between liquid, ice and vapour. Energy from the sun powers it. Water rises by evaporation and by transpiration from plants. It condenses into clouds and falls as precipitation, rain or snow. Some ice turns straight to vapour, which is called sublimation. On the ground, water soaks in, flows across the surface or moves underground. The ocean is the source of 86% of global evaporation. Most rain falls back into the ocean or onto land, where much of it flows over the ground as {{ref:nature-eco-275}}. That moving water does heavy work. It carries almost all eroded sediment and phosphorus from land to rivers, lakes and seas, and together with groundwater it carries nitrogen too. The cycle is essential to life and plays a large role in the global climate and ocean circulation.

nature-eco-176.title: The nitrogen cycle: plenty in the air, scarce in the soil
nature-eco-176.text: Nitrogen makes up 78% of the atmosphere, yet many ecosystems are starved of it. The gas is hard for living things to use, so usable nitrogen is scarce. The nitrogen cycle is the biogeochemical cycle in which nitrogen changes between chemical forms as it moves among the air, land and sea. Its main steps are {{ref:nature-eco-394}}, {{ref:nature-eco-178}}, {{ref:nature-eco-395}} and {{ref:nature-eco-396}}. Microbes carry out many of these steps, either harvesting energy or gathering nitrogen to grow. Plants take up two usable forms, nitrate and ammonium, from the soil through their root hairs. Because usable nitrogen is so scarce, its supply can set the pace of key ecosystem processes such as primary production and decomposition. People have changed this balance sharply. Growing legumes, making fertilizer with the {{ref:nature-eco-230}} and burning fuels have more than doubled the yearly conversion of nitrogen into forms life can use.

nature-eco-226.title: Evapotranspiration: how land breathes water back to the sky
nature-eco-226.text: Most of the rain and snow that lands on the continents never reaches a river. Globally, between three-fifths and three-quarters of it returns to the air through evapotranspiration. That is the combined movement of water into the air from open water, ice, bare soil and plants. The word joins two processes. Evaporation moves water straight into the air from soil and water bodies. Transpiration moves water from a plant's roots, up through the plant and out of its stomata, the tiny pores in its leaves, as vapour. Evapotranspiration is measured in millimetres of water over a set time. Three things mainly set its level. One is how much water is available. Another is how much energy is in the air and soil. The third is how much moisture the air can take up. Global warming has increased evapotranspiration over land, one of the ways a changing climate is altering the water cycle. The numbers matter in practice, because measuring evapotranspiration is key to managing water supplies and planning irrigation.

nature-eco-259.title: Soil carbon: a store three times the size of the atmosphere's
nature-eco-259.text: Soils store about 2,700 Gt of carbon, roughly three times the carbon in the atmosphere and 240 times a year's fossil fuel emissions. This soil carbon is the solid carbon held in soils, both as organic matter from living things and as carbonate minerals. It does daily work. It helps soil hold water, retain nutrients and build its crumbly structure. Photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition are the main processes that set how much carbon land stores. Because soil can take up carbon from the air, it matters for slowing global warming and for the computer models scientists use to project the climate. Human activities have caused a massive loss of organic carbon from soils, but people could also deliberately return carbon to them. Warming adds a risk of its own. It could change the activity of the soil microbes that break carbon down, possibly adding to the warming.

nature-eco-237.title: Infiltration: how rain soaks into the ground
nature-eco-237.text: Whether a storm waters a field or floods a street depends largely on one thing: how fast the ground can drink. Infiltration is the movement of water from the ground surface down into the soil. The fastest rate at which water can soak in is called the infiltration capacity, usually measured in meters per day. When rain falls faster than that, the extra water usually runs off over the surface. Texture matters. Soils with small pores, such as clay, take in water more slowly than soils with large pores, such as sand. Compaction squeezes the soil and lowers infiltration further. Wet soil soaks up water more slowly, and fully saturated soil cannot take in any more. Living things help. Plant roots and burrowing animals open cracks that speed water downward, while bare ground can have very low rates, which leads to runoff and erosion. Steeper slopes shed water more readily. Pavement and other impermeable surfaces stop infiltration entirely and send more water across the ground.

nature-eco-275.title: Surface runoff: when water cannot soak in
nature-eco-275.text: A roof or a parking lot lets no rain soak in at all. Every drop that lands becomes surface runoff, or overland flow. This is water flowing freely over the ground when rain, snowmelt or other water cannot soak into the soil fast enough. On natural ground, runoff starts when the soil is already saturated or when rain arrives faster than infiltration can take it in. Runoff is a major part of the water cycle. It is also the main way water wears soil away, the process covered in {{ref:nature-eco-264}}. Its main environmental harm is what it carries. Running water picks up petroleum, herbicides and fertilizers and delivers them into surface water, groundwater and soil. More runoff also means less water seeping down to refill groundwater, so water tables drop and droughts hit harder for people who rely on wells. When a stream cannot carry all the runoff flowing downstream, it floods. The remedies follow from the causes. Limit paved surfaces, control erosion on farms and building sites, build the green networks described in {{ref:nature-nbs-161}}, and control how chemicals are used.

nature-eco-264.title: Soil erosion: losing the ground under the crops
nature-eco-264.text: About 75 billion tons of soil erode from the land each year, some 13–40 times the natural rate. Soil erosion is the wearing away of the top layer of soil by water, ice, snow, wind, plants and animals, including people. It can be slow and unnoticed, or so fast that it causes a serious loss of topsoil. Farming is the main accelerator. Unsustainable farming raises erosion by one to two orders of magnitude, each a factor of ten, above the natural rate. That is far faster than new soil forms. On farms, erosion shrinks cropland and its production potential, lowers water quality and damages drainage networks. Erosion by water and wind together causes 84% of degraded land, and about 40% of the world's agricultural land is seriously degraded. Some soils resist better than others. Clay-rich and organic-rich soils hold together, and plant cover and roots protect soil from both water and wind. Longer, steeper slopes erode much faster in heavy rain, especially without plants. The outlook is not reassuring: the more intense rainfall expected as the climate warms will raise erosion unless measures are taken.

nature-eco-212.title: Cellular respiration: the slow burn inside every cell
nature-eco-212.text: Cellular respiration is technically a kind of burning, but one that releases energy slowly and under control. It is the process by which cells break down food molecules, usually with oxygen, to make ATP, the energy carrier cells use. With oxygen it is called aerobic respiration. When cells pass their electrons to some other substance instead, it is anaerobic. Aerobic respiration consumes glucose, a simple sugar, and oxygen, and it produces carbon dioxide, water and energy. In effect it releases the energy that photosynthesis stored in sugar. The oxygen route pays well: aerobic metabolism is up to 15 times more efficient than anaerobic metabolism. Current estimates put the yield at around 29 to 30 ATP per glucose molecule, below the textbook figure of 38. Plants respire too. Although they take in carbon dioxide overall, plant respiration produces about half of the carbon dioxide released each year by land ecosystems. The energy left after plants' own respiration is what ecologists call net primary production.

nature-eco-230.title: The Haber process: fertilizer pulled from the air
nature-eco-230.text: In 1909 Fritz Haber showed in his laboratory that nitrogen from the air could be turned into ammonia. Carl Bosch then scaled the method up for the company BASF. The Haber process, or Haber–Bosch process, remains the main industrial method of making ammonia from nitrogen in the air and hydrogen. It combines the two gases over an iron catalyst, a material that speeds the reaction. In effect it is nitrogen fixation done in a factory. Most of the ammonia goes into nitrogen fertilizer. The timing mattered. Demand for fertilizer was rising, and the mined niter and guano, or bird droppings, then in use were thought too scarce for future needs. The process still leans on fossil fuel. Its hydrogen usually comes from natural gas by steam reforming, which made 72% of global ammonia as of 2012. Ammonia production uses 1–2% of global energy, causes 3% of global carbon emissions and uses 3% to 5% of natural gas. As of 2018 it produced 230 million tonnes of ammonia a year.

nature-eco-185.title: The phosphorus cycle: the slow loop that skips the sky
nature-eco-185.text: Most of the great element cycles pass through the air. Phosphorus almost never does, because it rarely becomes a gas. The phosphorus cycle is the biogeochemical cycle that moves phosphorus through rocks, water and living things. Life cannot do without it. Phosphorus is part of DNA, RNA and ATP, and in animals it also strengthens bones and teeth. The cycle has four main steps. Rock that contains phosphorus is lifted up, then weathers and erodes. Rivers carry the phosphorus to lakes and the ocean, where it is finally buried in sediments. Phosphates, the compounds in which phosphorus usually travels, move quickly through plants and animals but very slowly through soil and ocean. That makes this one of the slowest biogeochemical cycles. On land, the slow release of phosphorus from weathering rock limits how much ecosystems can get. In water, phosphorus can limit the growth of aquatic life, so phosphates from fertilizers, sewage and detergents can pollute lakes and streams. Freshwater algal blooms, sudden mass growths of algae, are generally caused by excess phosphorus. Saltwater blooms tend to come from excess nitrogen.

nature-eco-245.title: Nutrient pollution: too much of a good thing
nature-eco-245.text: Nitrogen and phosphorus feed crops, but in a lake or a bay they become pollutants. Nutrient pollution is water pollution caused by too many nutrients, usually these two, entering water. It is a main cause of {{ref:nature-eco-216}} in lakes, rivers and coastal waters, where the extra nutrients feed algal growth. Sources include runoff from farms, septic tank waste, feedlots, raw sewage and emissions from burning fuels. Fertilizer that crops do not use is lost from fields and harms air and downstream water. In Europe, agriculture is usually the main source of nitrogen in water, while households and industry often dominate phosphorus. Excess nitrogen brings toxic algal blooms, oxygen-starved water, acidic rain, nitrogen-saturated forests and global warming. The costs are real: dearer water treatment, losses to commercial fishing, fishing for sport and shellfish, and less tourism income. Excess nitrate in drinking water can cause blue baby syndrome. Remedies include vegetated buffer strips, artificial wetlands, better wastewater treatment and permits that make the polluter pay.

nature-eco-216.title: Eutrophication: when a lake is fed too well
nature-eco-216.text: The word comes from the Greek eutrophos, meaning well-nourished, and that is exactly the trouble. Eutrophication is the build-up of nutrients in a body of water, causing extra growth of algae and plants that can use up the water's oxygen. It is caused by too much of a nutrient, most often phosphates and nitrates. It can happen naturally, or it can be caused by sewage, industrial wastewater, runoff carrying fertilizer and other human sources. Most of these nutrients arrive as the {{ref:nature-eco-245}} described earlier. The sequence is grimly simple. Extra nutrients feed a boom in phytoplankton. The resulting algal blooms and bacterial growth deplete the oxygen dissolved in the water, causing serious environmental damage. Fish die in larger numbers, and desirable species disappear. The problem is everywhere. Surveys found that 54% of lakes in Asia are eutrophic, along with 53% in Europe, 48% in North America, 41% in South America and 28% in Africa. Along the world's coasts, the {{ref:nature-hist-032}} has identified 375 zones where the water runs dangerously short of oxygen.

nature-eco-235.title: Hypoxia: when water runs short of oxygen
nature-eco-235.text: Most fish cannot live once water falls below 30% of the oxygen it could hold. Environmental hypoxia means low-oxygen conditions like this, usually in natural waters or in the thin air at altitude. Water with 1 to 30% of its possible oxygen saturation is called hypoxic, and water with none at all is anoxic. A healthy water body should seldom fall below 80%. The usual cause is nutrient pollution. Algal blooms die and sink, and the bacteria decomposing them use up the oxygen as they respire. Hypoxia can also happen without pollution. In estuaries, lighter river water can layer over seawater and block oxygen from reaching the bottom. Low oxygen is not bad for everything. It harms air-breathing organisms but is essential for many anaerobic ones, which live without oxygen.

nature-eco-214.title: Dead zones: stretches of sea where life suffocates
nature-eco-214.text: In 2017 the summer dead zone in the Gulf of Mexico covered over 22,000 square kilometres. Fertilizer washing off the land of the Mississippi basin had stripped its water of oxygen. Dead zones are low-oxygen areas in the world's oceans and large lakes where most aquatic life cannot survive. Hypoxia sets in when dissolved oxygen falls to 2 mg per litre or less, and mass die-offs follow below 0.5 mg per litre. The usual driver is eutrophication: extra nitrogen and phosphorus fuel algal blooms whose decay uses up the oxygen. Marine dead zones were first noted in the 1970s in heavily used waters such as Chesapeake Bay, the Baltic Sea and the Black Sea. A 2008 study counted 405 worldwide. Some are permanent, some last only hours or days, and many are seasonal, usually in summer and autumn. Warming makes them worse, because warmer water holds less oxygen, so dead zones are expanding. Recovery depends on how long and how severe the low oxygen was; after brief, mild events, life returns quickly.

nature-eco-201.title: Methane: a small gas with a big warming punch
nature-eco-201.text: Since about 1750, methane has made up just 3% of human heat-trapping gas emissions by mass, yet about 23% of their warming push on the climate. Atmospheric methane is the methane in Earth's air, a powerful heat-trapping gas whose rising level is driving the change described in {{ref:nature-hist-007}}. Its level has risen about 160% since 1750, almost entirely because of human activities. By 2025 the concentration had climbed from 722 parts per billion before industry to 1936 ppb, the highest in at least 800,000 years. Methane is potent but less persistent than carbon dioxide. Over 20 years it traps about 84 times as much heat as the same mass of carbon dioxide, but over 100 years only 28 times. It is the second largest contributor to human-caused warming. From 2010 to 2019, methane emissions caused 0.5 °C, about 30% of the warming seen. Wetlands are the largest natural source, providing roughly 20–30% of the methane in the air. Cutting methane by the end of the century could make a substantial difference to meeting the goals of the Paris climate agreement.

nature-eco-217.title: Cultural eutrophication: the human hand in green water
nature-eco-217.text: Cultural eutrophication is eutrophication caused by human activity. It became more visible in the mid-1900s, when the green revolution spread chemical fertilizers through farming. Phosphorus and nitrogen are its two main causes, letting algae grow fast and bloom densely. Laundry detergents were once a major phosphate source. They fed the problem until phosphate detergents were phased out in the 1970s, and since then sewage and agriculture have supplied most of the phosphate. Nitrogen comes mainly from farm runoff of fertilizer and animal waste, from sewage, and from nitrogen that settles out of the air. The label separates these cases from the slow enrichment that lakes undergo on their own, described in {{ref:nature-eco-218}}.

nature-eco-165.title: Carbon pools: where the planet keeps its carbon
nature-eco-165.text: Most of Earth's carbon is going nowhere. It sits inertly in the rocks of the lithosphere, the planet's rigid outer shell. Scientists usually split the global carbon cycle into major carbon pools, or reservoirs, linked by pathways of exchange. A pool is any part of the Earth system, such as the air, ocean or soil, where carbon is held in some form for a period of time. The pools include the ocean; sediments, including fossil fuels; living things on land and their soils; the atmosphere; and the rocks of the geosphere. The deep ocean is the largest pool of actively cycled carbon, holding 50 times more than the atmosphere. Yet it exchanges carbon with the surface only over hundreds of years. About a third of soil carbon is stored in inorganic forms such as calcium carbonate. Pool is the broader term: {{ref:nature-eco-169}} is one particular kind of pool.

nature-eco-169.title: Carbon sinks: the places that soak up carbon
nature-eco-169.text: A forest or an ocean does something no machine yet does at large scale: it pulls carbon out of the sky faster than it lets carbon go. Such a store is a carbon sink, a carbon pool, natural or artificial, that takes up more carbon from the atmosphere than it releases. Sinks are an important part of the natural carbon cycle. Globally, the two most important are vegetation and the ocean. Soils hold more carbon than all land plants and the atmosphere together, but heavy, industrial farming has severely depleted the carbon in many agricultural soils. For gases other than carbon dioxide, a sink need not store anything. It can break the gas down, as when nitrous oxide is reduced to harmless nitrogen gas. Artificial sinks store carbon in building materials or deep underground. Still, no major artificial system yet removes carbon from the air on a large scale. Meanwhile, deforestation and industrial agriculture have depleted natural sinks, and this change in land use is one cause of global warming. Public awareness of sinks grew after the 1997 treaty described in {{ref:nature-clim-056}} promoted their use to offset emissions.

nature-eco-171.title: Helping forests, soils and seas store more carbon
nature-eco-171.text: Two of the most powerful tools for cutting emissions before 2030 are simple: restoring ecosystems and converting less land. Enhancing natural carbon sinks means managing forests, soils and other ecosystems so they remove more carbon dioxide from the air and store it durably. Preserving and strengthening sinks is an important way to slow global warming. It requires changes in farming and forestry, such as preventing deforestation and restoring ecosystems by replanting trees. The 2022 IPCC report calls these land-based options AFOLU mitigation, short for agriculture, forestry and other land use. Ocean methods such as seaweed farming and fertilising the sea have been proposed, but none has yet been used at large scale.

nature-nbs-103.title: Forests as carbon sinks, and why they may falter
nature-nbs-103.text: Each year the world's forests take up about 25% of the carbon people emit. Through photosynthesis they draw carbon dioxide from the air and store it as wood, roots and leaves. That service is weakening. In 2019 forests absorbed a third less carbon than in the 1990s, because of higher temperatures, droughts and deforestation. Forests can switch from sinks to sources of carbon, and the typical forest in the tropics may become a source by the 2060s. Storage is also conditional: carbon stays out of the air only if trees are not burned and do not rot when they die. New forests take several decades to match the carbon benefit of keeping mature forests standing. Clearing and later replanting also causes lasting losses of wildlife and damage to soil. So scientists call protecting natural forests the major climate solution. How much new tree cover could help is disputed. One estimate of 0.9 billion hectares of extra canopy has been criticised as too high, once the effect of trees on reflected sunlight is counted.

nature-eco-166.title: Two speeds of carbon: years and millions of years
nature-eco-166.text: A carbon atom can pass through a plant and back into the air within years. Another can stay locked in rock for millions. Carbon moves in a fast cycle through living things and a slow cycle through rocks. The fast, biological cycle carries carbon from the air into living things and back again. The slow, geological cycle moves carbon through the crust between rocks, soil, ocean and air. It may even reach deep into the mantle, the hot layer beneath the crust. Each matters in its own way. How the fast cycle responds to human activity will decide many of the more immediate impacts of global warming. The slow cycle, for all its slowness, is one of the most important controls on how much carbon is in the air, and so on global temperatures.

nature-eco-168.title: How people knocked the carbon cycle off balance
nature-eco-168.text: As of 2020, people had extracted about 450 gigatons of fossil carbon from the ground, nearly as much as is held in all living things on land. Since the Industrial Revolution, human activity has greatly disturbed the carbon cycle by moving huge amounts of carbon out of the ground. Extracting and burning fossil fuels moves carbon straight from rock into the air. It is the largest human impact and one of the fastest growing. Cement adds more, because heating limestone to make clinker, cement's raw material, releases carbon dioxide. Clearing forests for farms or cities releases carbon from land ecosystems into the air. That clearing also cuts biodiversity, weakening ecosystems' resilience and their ability to pull carbon from the air. Small amounts of halocarbon gases caused about 10% of the direct warming effect of long-lived heat-trapping gases in 2019. For now, the rest of the Earth system cushions the blow. Carbon exchanges between the air and the land and sea act as negative feedbacks, changes that push back, dampening the climate effect of human emissions.

openers.cycles-of-carbon-water-and-nutrients: Nothing in the living world is ever truly used up. The carbon, water and nitrogen in a leaf or a fish have passed through air, rock, soil and sea before, and they will again. This chapter follows those loops, the biogeochemical cycles that move elements between living things, the air and the Earth's crust. It starts with photosynthesis, which turns sunlight into chemical energy, and cellular respiration, which releases it again. Then it traces rain that soaks in, runs off and carries soil away, the carbon stored in soils, and the human hand on the nitrogen cycle, from the Haber process that makes ammonia out of air onward.
